tasks.question: A platform sells a tenant 100 requests per second but enforces it with a 100-token-per-second bucket in each of six replicas. Under uneven routing the tenant exceeds the sold rate, and during a quota-store outage the replicas keep admitting. Why is the sold limit not enforced, and what must the limiter contract state about scope, accounting failure and the difference between rate and concurrency?
tasks.answer:
# Why the sold limit is not enforced

**Direct answer.** The sold limit is a tenant-scoped promise; the limiter enforces a
replica-scoped budget. Six independent 100-token/s buckets do not compose into a 100/s
cap, they define an envelope of up to 600 admissions/s whose real value depends on
routing, replica count and, during a quota-store outage, on whichever permissive
fallback each replica chooses. No component holds the tenant's aggregate, so the sold
number is never the object being counted. The outage does not create the gap; it
removes the only place where the gap could have been detected and corrected. The
limiter contract therefore has to state three things explicitly: the enforced scope
and its owner, the accounting-failure behavior with a numeric overshoot budget and a
reconciliation rule, and rate, concurrency and queue limits as separate dimensions
with units, deadlines and enforcement points.

## 1. Scope: the limit is enforced on the wrong object

A token bucket is a budget for one accounting scope. The platform sells a budget for
the tenant and configures a bucket for the process. Those are different objects, so
the deployment's replica count becomes an undeclared multiplier: with N replicas the
aggregate allowance is at most N x 100 tokens/s, and the book states the general rule
- four replicas independently granting the same bucket approach four times the
intended scope, because a per-instance bucket's aggregate allowance "changes with
replicas and routing" (admission-resource#local-limits). Scaling out from six to seven
replicas would raise the sold 100/s to 700/s without any contract change; a canary
deployment adds a seventh budget for its lifetime.

The book names the alternatives and their prices: "A global quota needs atomic shared
accounting, coordinated budget leases or a deliberately documented approximation."
Each choice moves the problem rather than deleting it. A central atomic bucket buys an
explicit shared scope and pays with quota-store latency, hot-key behavior and a new
availability dependency. Leased local budgets reduce shared operations but must "never
grant overlapping spend" and must account for unused or lost allocations. Approximate
distributed counts scale but must bound the permitted overshoot and name the invariant
they protect. The current design has taken the per-instance row of that table, which
gives local protection and no tenant guarantee, while advertising the tenant-level
promise.

There is a second scope error underneath. Admission has to precede the expensive
operation and protect the resource that actually caps useful completed work; more
application instances "do not relax a shared database quota or single-key transaction
bottleneck" (admission-resource#1). If the sold 100/s protects a downstream dependency
or a cost envelope, then six local buckets protect six CPUs and nothing else. The
limit is enforced where it is cheap to enforce, not where the scarce resource or the
billing commitment lives.

## 2. Routing decides how far above 100 the ceiling sits

Let B = 100 tokens/s per replica and let the tenant's offered rate be lambda, split
across replicas with shares p_i. Admitted throughput is approximately
sum over i of min(B, p_i x lambda). That expression has a wide range:

- all traffic to one replica: 100/s, the only routing that happens to match the sale;
- lambda = 600 spread evenly over six replicas: 600/s, six times the sold rate;
- lambda = 600 with a 50/30/20 split over three replicas: 100 + 100 + 100 = 300/s;
- first rejection appears only when p_max x lambda > 100, so with a 50% hot replica
  the tenant is not throttled until roughly 200/s - twice what it bought.

Routing is not a stable input. Selectors that balance connection counts can still
produce a 90/1/1 request split (discovery-balancing#original-worked-design), affinity
"may overload one backend when a key becomes hot", and each client "sees only a
partial view" of unfinished work elsewhere. Sticky sessions reduce movement but are
"not a failover proof" (session-consistency#failure-cost-and-alternatives). A tenant
pinned to one replica consumes one bucket and is safe by accident; the same tenant
after a rebalance or failover is served by three replicas and its ceiling triples.
The limiter's behavior is therefore a function of a component it does not own and
cannot observe.

The result is the worst of both directions. Under spread, the tenant exceeds the sold
rate and the platform cannot see it, because the evidence is also partitioned: each
replica's counters look compliant. Under skew, capacity is stranded on idle replicas
while the hot one rejects - and with a bucket capacity smaller than an instantaneous
burst, even a conforming tenant can be rejected at the hot replica while its aggregate
is at or below 100/s. Unused tokens on idle replicas are not transferable, so the sale
is both unenforceable as a ceiling and unreliable as a guarantee.

## 3. Accounting failure: the outage removes the only possible check

A quota store is not automatically in the admission path. If replicas hold their own
buckets and consult the store only to refresh counts, then the store's outage changes
nothing observable: the replicas keep admitting at the old per-replica rate because a
local bucket is a permission, not a check. That is exactly the described symptom. It
also means the system has two indistinguishable states - normal operation, already up
to six times over the sold rate, and outage, still up to six times over - so the
outage is a visibility failure, not the root cause.

If the store is authoritative, the outage forces a choice the contract must already
have made. For a quota protecting a hard external limit, unavailable shared accounting
"may require rejecting new work or using only a known unused local allocation"
(admission-resource#local-limits). The book is explicit that "a shared limiter adds a
dependency; its timeout must not become permission to spend an unlimited budget", and
that the permitted overshoot and the recovery reconciliation must be stated, because
"the labels fail-open/fail-closed do not answer this design question." A fallback on
the quota path is a degraded admission mode, and the resilience evidence says a
fallback "can hide the outage" and must have a defined fail-fast or fallback contract
(circuit-breaker#overview).

Concretely, the failure clause needs: the authority that counts; the timeout and
error classes that count as "accounting unavailable"; the degraded ceiling (reject
beyond a pre-granted unused lease, or a fixed fraction such as B/N per replica, or a
single declared fleet-wide cap); the maximum overshoot in requests and in time; how
unused, lost and duplicated leases are accounted so that spend never overlaps; and
how counts reconcile on recovery so that the return of the store does not create a
synchronized refill and retry wave - "randomized backoff must not cause all replicas
to refill and retry in the same wave." Reopening budgets is itself a recovery policy:
a controlled ramp with per-tenant limits and hysteresis, not one global switch.

## 4. Rate is not concurrency

The two limits constrain different populations. A token bucket "constrains arrival
over time according to configured tokens and burst capacity; a concurrency semaphore
limits simultaneous resident work. These solve related but different problems.
Neither prevents unbounded work within the other dimension unless combined with
deadlines and measured downstream budgets" (admission-resource#3). A concurrency cap
"limits resident work" and requires permits to be released after termination, with
stuck work distinguished from completed work (admission-resource#1).

The arithmetic is Little's law, L = lambda x W. At a fixed 100/s admission and a mean
0.15 s, 15 requests are in flight (the book's own example: 200/s at 0.15 s gives 30).
If latency rises to 1.5 s at the same 100/s, 150 requests are in flight and the
downstream pool is exhausted while the rate limiter reports perfect compliance. That
is why a connection pool "is a limit on concurrent access" and says nothing about how
long each transaction holds a connection (fleet-budgets#1), and why a fleet of four
instances with 25 connections each is a 100-connection bound that becomes 125 with a
fifth replica. The concurrency dimension has the same scope bug as the rate
dimension: six replicas times a per-replica permit count is the real fleet permit
count.

A 100 rps sale also says nothing about cost. Operations with unequal costs cannot be
controlled solely by requests per second (admission-resource#2), and the book models
work units where an operation costs five units against a 20-unit/s refill, so a
"request" limit can still admit six times the intended resource. The contract must
state whether the unit is requests, work units or both, and how estimated and actual
cost reconcile without letting a client choose an artificially cheap class.

## 5. What the limiter contract must state

1. **Subject and scope.** The tenant (and route, class or method) is the accounting
   subject; name the component that enforces it and the aggregation rule. If
   enforcement is per replica, write N into the contract and state that the effective
   cap is N x B and how N changes under autoscaling, canaries, failover and
   rebalancing.
2. **Unit and cost.** Requests, work units or weighted cost; how cost is estimated,
   reconciled and bounded; whether rejected and retried work consumes the budget
   (retries must consume the same tenant budget, not a fresh one).
3. **Rate semantics.** Refill rate, bucket capacity (the burst bound, since admitted
   cost is at most capacity + rate x t only if a single logical bucket is enforced),
   measurement window, clock source and skew tolerance, and whether the limit applies
   at admission or at completion.
4. **Concurrency semantics.** Maximum resident work, permit acquisition and release
   on every termination path including cancellation and timeout, plus a bounded queue
   with both a maximum item count and a maximum age.
5. **Deadline.** The per-request deadline that makes a late admission useless; a fast
   rejection is safer than admitting work that cannot finish, but it must not be
   reported as success.
6. **Accounting authority and mechanism.** Atomic shared counter, non-overlapping
   leases with explicit accounting for unused and lost allocations, or a documented
   approximation with its bound; hot-key behavior and store latency budget.
7. **Accounting failure.** Degraded ceiling, permitted overshoot in requests and
   time, reconciliation on recovery, hysteresis before reopening, and the invariant
   that timeout is never permission to spend an unlimited budget.
8. **Rejection contract.** Which work was not accepted, whether a retry can help, how
   long to wait, and retry guidance consistent with the remaining budget and deadline
   so that every client does not immediately recreate the overload.
9. **Fairness.** Per-tenant outstanding work and maximum age, how spare capacity may
   be borrowed, reservation for quiet tenants, and authenticated priority that cannot
   starve ordinary work.
10. **Observability.** Offered, rejected, admitted and correctly completed work per
    tenant and class; queue age; shared-store failures; aggregate admitted cost
    compared with the sold value, not only per-replica success rates. Per-replica
    quantiles cannot be averaged into a global view and counters need reset-aware
    deltas (metric-semantics#2).
11. **Change control and acceptance.** Who may raise a limit, how the change is
    published atomically across replicas, and the tests: route one tenant across all
    replicas, change the replica count, partition the quota store, duplicate a lease,
    cancel admitted work, restart a permit owner, and verify actual aggregate admitted
    cost, bounded overshoot and progress for a quiet tenant. The book's own limitation
    is that these are proposed tests, with "no load test or distributed-limiter
    execution performed" (admission-resource#local-limits).

## 6. Boundaries and trade-offs

- **Per-replica limits are not wrong; using them as the tenant cap is.** Each replica
  still needs a local guard for its own CPU, memory and pool. The design needs both
  layers and must not present the local one as the sold one.
- **Central accounting is not free.** A single atomic bucket has correct scope but
  adds a synchronous dependency and a hot key; the store becomes part of the
  availability budget. That is why leases and approximations exist, but they are only
  honest when their overshoot bound is stated and monitored.
- **Leases trade precision for load.** Fewer shared operations, but unused
  allocations are stranded, lost leases are spend, and the lease quantity times the
  replica count is the real ceiling during normal operation.
- **Pinning a tenant to one placement can make per-replica equal per-tenant**, but
  only while the mapping is authoritative and stable; failover, rebalance, autoscaling
  or a stale placement cache restores the multiplier, and pinning trades availability
  for enforcement.
- **The right failure mode depends on the protected invariant.** If 100/s protects a
  hard external quota or a contractual penalty, reject rather than overspend; if it is
  a fairness knob for a best-effort feature, a bounded degraded ceiling may be
  acceptable. The contract must say which, with numbers.
- **The labels are not the design.** Fail-open and fail-closed describe a default, not
  an overshoot bound, a reconciliation rule or a recovery ramp.
- **The evidence does not establish this platform's facts.** The book's page is
  source-linked for the mechanisms, but its bucket arithmetic is invented and
  self-reviewed, not measured; it supports the reasoning, not a claim about this
  deployment's actual traffic.

## Facet matrix and search record

| Facet | Queries | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| F1 scope | quota per tenant; global limit across replicas | admission-resource local |
| F2 routing | per-instance limit; routing skew; hot shard | discovery-balancing; multitenant |
| F3 failure | fail open; permitted overshoot; stale budget | admission-resource; breaker |
| F4 rate vs conc. | in-flight; bucket burst; Little's law | admission-resource 3; fleet 1 |
| F5 contract | limiter contract units scope failure | admission-resource; multitenant |
| F6 verify | per-replica metrics; replica skew | admission-resource; metric-semantics |

Two closing search rounds (quota enforcement at the resource; oversell promised
capacity; limit scope mismatch process versus tenant; rate limiter shared state
counter atomic) added no section beyond those listed, which is the stopping
condition used.

## Evidence map

- Sold 100/s is tenant-scoped; per-instance buckets give up to N x 100/s and change
  with replicas and routing -> admission-resource#local-limits.
- Global scope requires atomic accounting, leases or a documented approximation ->
  admission-resource#local-limits.
- A shared limiter's timeout must not become permission to spend ->
  admission-resource#local-limits.
- Accounting unavailability: reject or spend only known unused allocation; state
  permitted overshoot; fail-open/fail-closed labels are insufficient ->
  admission-resource#local-limits.
- Token bucket vs semaphore bound different dimensions; neither bounds the other ->
  admission-resource#3.
- Concurrency cap limits resident work; release permits; stuck vs completed ->
  admission-resource#1.
- Bucket bound is capacity + rate x t under one logical bucket ->
  admission-resource#local-limits.
- Pool size is a concurrency limit; duration matters; N replicas multiply it ->
  fleet-budgets#1.
- L = lambda x W; in-flight grows with latency at fixed rate -> workload-shape#2.
- Selector can produce 90/1/1; affinity overloads a hot backend; partial view ->
  discovery-balancing#original-worked-design.
- Sticky sessions are not a failover proof -> session-consistency#failure-cost.
- Skew makes headroom unusable; do not spread an overloaded tenant fleet-wide ->
  multitenant#resource-arithmetic; multitenant#proposed-acceptance.
- Contract promises a bounded deadline or explicit overload; per-tenant budgets ->
  multitenant#workload-and-service-contract.
- Quotas must be enforceable and observable at the resource; quota bypass is the
  failure mode -> tenant-based-resource-isolation#overview.
- Fallback can hide an outage; fallback contract must be defined ->
  circuit-breaker#overview.
- Rejection needs retry guidance and declared quotas; track offered/rejected/admitted
  and shared-store failures -> overload#purpose-and-mission;
  admission-resource#local-limits.
- Proposed tests: route across all replicas, change replica count, partition store,
  duplicate lease; no execution performed -> admission-resource#local-limits.
- Per-replica quantiles cannot be averaged; reset-aware counters ->
  metric-semantics#2.

## Unknowns and confidence

Unknown: the bucket capacity per replica (only the 100/s refill is given), so the
burst bound and the possibility of rejecting a conforming tenant remain unresolved.
Unknown: whether the quota store is authoritative for admission or only for reporting,
which determines whether the outage is a visibility failure or an active fail-open.
Unknown: whether 100/s is a guaranteed capacity or a ceiling, whether billing counts
offered or admitted requests, whether N is fixed, and what downstream resource the 100
protects. Unknown: whether the tenant is pinned by placement, and whether an edge
layer already sees all of its traffic.

Confidence is high on the mechanism: per-replica budgets cannot enforce a tenant cap,
the ceiling is sum of min(B, p_i x lambda), and a rate limit does not bound
concurrency. Confidence is medium on the recommended design point (central accounting
or leases plus a bounded degraded mode), because it depends on the store's availability
budget and the downstream invariant. Confidence is low on any numeric claim about this
platform's actual behavior: the book's arithmetic is synthetic and no distributed
limiter was executed. What would change the answer: evidence of a tenant-scoped
gateway with shared accounting, a fixed one-tenant-per-replica placement, or a quota
store whose outage is already fail-closed with a stated overshoot - each would move
the diagnosis from scope mismatch to a narrower failure-contract defect.
core_claims: A 100-token-per-second bucket deployed in each of six replicas creates six independent local allowances rather than one shared 100-per-second limit, so under uneven routing the tenant can exceed the sold rate and the aggregate can approach 600 admitted requests per second.

The sold 100-per-second rate is a tenant-global scope claim, while a per-instance bucket enforces only a local scope; a global quota requires atomic shared accounting, coordinated budget leases, or an explicitly documented bounded approximation.

When the quota store is unavailable, the limiter contract must either reject new work to protect the hard limit or spend only a known unused local allocation; a limiter timeout must not become permission to admit unlimited work.

The contract must state the permitted overshoot during an accounting outage and the reconciliation rule for restoring the shared budget, because fail-open and fail-closed labels do not answer that design question.

A token bucket bounds admitted cost over an interval while a concurrency semaphore bounds work resident at one time, and neither controls the other dimension without deadlines, measured downstream budgets, and a queue bounded by both item count and maximum age.

The contract must define the acceptance boundary: rejection before acceptance is not durable work, accepted-pending is not completed, and an outcome unknown after a possible commit must be reconciled by stable identity rather than retried blindly.
optional_claims: The limiter must track offered, admitted, rejected, completed and failed work separately per tenant and class, and measure the rejection path itself, because refusals also consume parsing, authentication, logging and retry capacity.

A single shared FIFO can be filled by one tenant even when average capacity is sufficient, so admission must bound per-tenant outstanding work and maximum age and declare how spare capacity may be borrowed.
Leased local budgets must never grant overlapping spend and must account for unused or lost allocations when reconciling with the shared quota.

judge_0.notes: Thorough and well-supported on replica-scope versus tenant-scope limits, quota-store failure and rate-versus-concurrency, though the acceptance-boundary core claim is only partly addressed (rejection and admission-versus-completion semantics, no stable-identity reconciliation).

judge_1.notes: Scope, routing, outage accounting and rate-versus-concurrency are strong, but the acceptance-boundary claim (rejected versus accepted-pending versus unknown-after-commit reconciliation by stable identity) is not addressed, so core coverage is partial.

tasks.question: A team resharding from 16 to 17 modulo buckets finds that nearly every key remaps, so it adopts a consistent-hashing ring and raises virtual nodes per node from 64 to 512. Why does the ring bound movement, and why can more tokens still worsen failure and repair outcomes rather than making ownership safer?
tasks.answer:
# Q206 — Why a consistent-hashing ring bounds movement, and why more tokens can still worsen failure and repair

## 1. Direct answer

Modulo sharding makes ownership a function of the bucket count itself: a key goes to hash(key) mod N, so changing N changes the function for almost every key. Going from 16 to 17 buckets keeps a key only when its hash is congruent both modulo 16 and modulo 17, which means congruent modulo lcm(16,17)=272; about 1/272 of keys (roughly 0.37%) stay, so roughly 99.6% move. A consistent-hashing ring makes ownership a property of positions on a circle instead: a key belongs to the first node clockwise from its hash. Inserting or removing one node therefore changes ownership only inside the arc that node takes over or vacates, so the expected moved share is about K/N — about 1/17, or 5.9%, when the 17th node joins — not the whole keyspace.

Virtual nodes are a balance knob, not a safety knob. Raising tokens per node from 64 to 512 smooths each node's share of the ring (relative deviation falls roughly with the square root of the token count), but it does not change the expected moved fraction on a join or leave, and it multiplies the number of ownership ranges that a failure must reassign, that hinted handoff and anti-entropy repair must track, and that a topology change may move at once. More tokens can therefore improve average balance while worsening blast radius, reassignment pacing and repair tail. Ownership safety comes from fencing, ownership epochs, verified handoff and bounded reassignment, not from token count.

## 2. Facet matrix (six facets)

| Facet | Question it answers | Query formulations used | Primary evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| F1 Modulo remap | Why 16 to 17 buckets moves nearly every key | resharding; modulo bucket remap; keyspace remap fraction | P (modulo paragraph) |
| F2 Ring bound | Why a ring moves only a fraction | consistent hashing; hash ring; token ring | P (invariant paragraph); CARD |
| F3 Token count and balance | What 64 to 512 vnodes actually buys | virtual nodes; tokens per node; partition count | P (mechanism); CARD good-fit |
| F4 Failure outcomes | Why more tokens can worsen node loss | hot token range; ring membership gossip; vnodes | P (failure paragraph); QUORUM; CELLS-F |
| F5 Repair outcomes | Why more tokens can worsen repair and rebuild | anti-entropy repair; hinted handoff; Merkle tree | QUORUM; P (runbook); CASE |
| F6 Boundaries and safety | When the ring does not bound movement, and what safety requires | ownership epoch; fencing stale ownership; shard key | SHARD; STRAT1; STRAT3; CELLS-P |

P = tycho.page.94165346d83c4ff79634d4400f4a9ba7#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes (Resharding and alternatives).
CARD = tycho.page.ba4ee752a40342cfb6d6be5ac81c4bd3#overview (Consistent Hashing card).
QUORUM = tycho.page.b93c892861fb4dd4afcfbdc2ced1af80#bounded-pattern-ownership-notes (Replica properties and quorum failure envelopes).
CELLS-P = ...cells-and-shuffle-shards-solve-different-placement-questions; CELLS-F = ...failure-and-recovery-policies (Cells and shuffle sharding).
CASE = tycho.page.b55f5bf29d7946c78454a769980c476e#what-changed-in-the-migration-plan (Discord storage migration).
SHARD = tycho.page.0d34dd26886340b89fd4f1499d790a81#purpose-and-mission (Sharding, partition keys, hotspots and safe resharding).
STRAT1 = tycho.page.3b048fab91c24b9f8121564b9b0e59bb#1-distinguish-physical-partitions-logical-ownership-and-replicas (Partition ownership, keys and skew).
STRAT3 = tycho.page.3b048fab91c24b9f8121564b9b0e59bb#3-four-partition-strategies-and-their-drawbacks (Partition ownership, keys and skew).

## 3. Mechanism and justification

### F1. Why 16 to 17 modulo buckets remaps almost everything

Modulo hashing assigns a key to hash(key) mod N, so the owner is a function of the modulus. The book records the consequence directly: 'Modulo hashing assigns a key to hash(key) mod N. Cassandra says adding one node "might invalidate almost all of the mappings"; Karger et al. describe the same central-redistribution problem for classical hash functions when machines join.' The same section's choice rule is 'use modulo only when N is fixed.'

Arithmetic (my derivation in support of that source claim, not a measured result): a key keeps its bucket across 16 and 17 only if its hash h satisfies h mod 16 = h mod 17, which requires h to be congruent modulo lcm(16,17) = 272. Only about 1/272 of hash values, roughly 0.37%, survive; about 99.6% move. The failure is structural, not a tuning mistake: 16 and 17 are coprime, so the modulus itself changes for nearly every key, and nothing about the key's current placement predicts its new placement. Client caches, routing tables and in-flight writes all become stale at once, which is exactly the 'central redistribution' problem the ring was invented to avoid.

### F2. Why the ring bounds movement

The ring decouples ownership from node count. The book's mechanism summary: 'A consistent hash function maps keys and nodes into one circular space. A key belongs to the first node encountered clockwise from its hash position, and each physical node normally claims many small positions, called tokens or virtual nodes, rather than one large arc.' A new node inserted at a position takes only the keys whose clockwise predecessor changed — the arc between the previous owner and the new position. Everything else keeps its successor node.

The book's invariant paragraph states the bound: 'With K keys spread over N equal-share nodes, adding or removing one node should move about K/N keys: the joining or leaving node's share, not the whole keyspace.' It supports this with Dynamo ('departure or arrival "only affects its immediate neighbors"'), Cassandra ('only has to move a small fraction of the keys'), Riak ('1/(number of nodes) of the ring') and Karger et al. ('the minimum needed to maintain a balanced load'). At 16 to 17 nodes the expected moved share is about 1/17 = 5.9%, versus the roughly 99.6% of modulo — about a seventeenfold difference in moved keys (my arithmetic).

The book is careful about the status of that number: 'The ~1/N figure is an expectation under balance, not a guarantee,' and Tycho's rule is to 'measure the actual moved fraction, because random tokens, unequal vnode counts and hot keys can exceed the ideal share.' So the ring bounds movement under stated assumptions (balance, unchanged hash, unchanged token layout); it is not a proof for any particular cluster.

### F3. What 64 to 512 virtual nodes actually buys

One token per node gives each node one large arc; arc sizes are random, so node shares vary widely. Many tokens per node replace one big arc with many small arcs, so a node's share is a sum of many small random pieces and clusters closer to the mean. That is the balance argument, and it is the reason the number of tokens is called out as an owned parameter: ring, 'token/vnode count and replication factor are owned; key and token distribution are measured' (card good-fit conditions), and 'uneven token ranges produce uneven request load' (P).

Quantitatively (my model, not a book measurement): if a node holds k independent arcs, its share has relative standard deviation on the order of 1/sqrt(k). At k=64 that is about 12.5%; at k=512 about 4.4%. Going from 64 to 512 therefore cuts relative imbalance by roughly a factor of 2.8. What it does not do is change the expected moved fraction on a join or leave: that stays about 1/(N+1) regardless of k, because the moved set is still the arcs the entering or leaving node owns. Token count trades variance for granularity, not variance for movement.

The same 8x increase also multiplies the number of ranges: at 17 nodes, 64 tokens gives about 1,088 ranges and 512 tokens about 8,704 (my arithmetic). Each range is a unit of ownership, transfer, hinting and repair, which is where F4 and F5 come from.

### F4. Why more tokens can worsen failure outcomes

A node loss with k tokens is not one transfer; it is k ownership transfers, each with its own replica set, hinted-handoff stream and streaming job. Dynamo's approach, as summarized in the book, 'disperses an unavailable node's load across remaining nodes and sends missed replicas to a hinted node; when the node recovers, hinted replicas are delivered and anti-entropy repairs permanent divergence.' Dispersal is finer with 512 tokens, so no single successor absorbs a large arc — good for post-failure balance. But the count of transfers, hint streams and affected peers grows with k, and the failure is now smeared across many peers instead of concentrated on a few.

The book records the counterweight explicitly: 'Cassandra warns that each token adds failure combinations and raises outage probability,' and Tycho's runbook says to 'bound token counts against repair and outage cost.' The card repeats the same warning in compressed form: 'Cassandra warns that more tokens raise outage probability and maintenance cost.' The mechanism (my inference from the sources, not a quantified source claim) is that with more ranges the number of distinct replica sets and in-flight range movements grows, so a second failure or a topology change overlaps more partially moved ranges; each overlap is small, but their sum can exceed survivor headroom. The cells page states the general control for exactly this: 'A cell outage needs reserved recovery capacity, a reconstructible durable state path, and a bounded reassignment rate. Moving every tenant immediately can exhaust survivors.' Applying that to tokens (my transfer) means reassigning 512 ranges per lost node takes more pacing than 64, so recovery is longer and needs more reserved capacity.

There is also a correctness hazard, not only a capacity hazard: 'Cassandra warns that simultaneous range movements can "violate monotonic consistency and can even cause data loss"' (QUORUM, reporting Cassandra's warning). More ranges per node means more range movements in flight during any membership change, which widens that window.

So more tokens do not make ownership safer: they make load more even and failures more fragmented. 'Safer' would require fewer simultaneous movements, better fencing and sufficient recovery capacity — none of which token count supplies.

### F5. Why more tokens can worsen repair and rebuild outcomes

Repair is per range. The book: 'hinted handoff and Merkle-tree anti-entropy repair lagging replicas,' while read repair and hinted handoff are 'only best-effort' and anti-entropy is what provides eventual consistency (QUORUM). Hinted handoff is temporary protection, not repair (CARD, P). With 8x more ranges, the number of Merkle-tree comparisons, validation compactions, repair sessions and stream setups grows roughly 8x, while the data per range falls roughly 8x. Fixed per-range costs — scheduling, tree construction, session bookkeeping, streaming setup, compaction overhead — do not shrink with the range, so total repair work per byte grows as ranges get smaller (my inference; the book states the mechanism and the direction, not a cost curve).

Rebuild after failure inherits the same granularity. A rebuilding node must receive hundreds of small ranges from many peers instead of a few large ones; more peers, more sessions, more chances of a straggler. The Discord case is the book's concrete demonstration of per-range tail risk: the token-range migrator 'stalled near 99.9999% on ranges full of uncompacted tombstones,' and the book's lesson is that 'a fraction of token ranges can contain disproportionate scan work, deletion markers and operational risk' and that treating 99.9999% as a completeness certificate would have produced false acceptance. More ranges means more tail samples and more chances that some range is pathological; the tail is per range, so splitting ranges multiplies the number of tails to clear.

### F6. What safety actually requires, and when the ring does not bound movement

The book's safety conditions are about authority and verification, not tokens: the card's good-fit list requires that 'the ring, token/vnode count and replication factor are owned' and that 'a rebalance and repair path exists' and 'ownership can be fenced during a change.' Tycho's runbook says to 'record the ownership epoch at every membership change,' and warns that 'a ring without epoch fencing can still route one key to two owners during a change.' The sharding page's invariant is the same: a versioned shard map assigns each key to a shard, 'one authoritative owner must exist per key, and a resharding move must fence writes or preserve a verifiable handoff' (SHARD).

Three boundaries limit the 1/N claim. First, it covers a single node join or leave under a fixed hash and token layout; changing token counts from 64 to 512 is itself a layout change, and unless new tokens are placed inside each node's existing arcs the movement can exceed the ideal share — hence 'measure the actual moved fraction.' Second, changing the hash function invalidates stability entirely: the shard-key table says the routing function 'does not guarantee stability through routing/hash algorithm changes' (STRAT1). Third, the ring balances keys, not load: the hash-strategy row warns 'single hot key still hot' (STRAT3), and hot spots are the failure the original paper targets (the book notes the Karger title names 'Relieving Hot Spots'). A hot key stays on one owner at 64 or 512 tokens.

Finally, a hash does not create independence: 'Do not assume assignments are statistically independent just because they use a hash. Capacity skew, placement constraints, correlated failure and retries all change overlap and impact' (CELLS-P). That is the precise sense in which more tokens can look safer (better average balance) while leaving correlated-failure exposure and blast radius untouched.

## 4. Boundaries and trade-offs

- The ring vs modulo contrast is a movement contrast, not a completeness claim. The book's alternative section also lists explicit range assignment (operator control, range locality, manual planning) and rendezvous/highest-random-weight hashing (no shared ring), and its choice rule says to 'reverse the choice when ring operations and virtual-node tuning cost more than the movement they save' — which is exactly the 64 to 512 question.
- Token count is a cost/benefit dial with two failure directions: too few tokens leaves lumps (large arcs, skewed load, coarse repair units); too many multiplies per-range overhead, failure combinations, concurrent movements and repair tail. The card's own rule is to 'bound token counts against repair and outage cost', not to maximize them.
- The binding constraint on a failure is often survivor headroom, not ring geometry: recovery needs 'reserved recovery capacity' and a 'bounded reassignment rate' (CELLS-F). A 512-token node failure is 512 reassignments to pace; whether that is better or worse than 64 depends on transfer parallelism and per-transfer overhead, which the book does not measure.
- The evidence is documentation- and paper-grounded, not benchmarked: the resharding page states its sources are 'public papers and documentation, not benchmarks' and that Tycho-labelled rules are synthesis. No cluster, rebalance or migration was run (SHARD source limits). So the qualitative mechanism is well supported; the specific 64/512 comparison is a modeled argument.
- The 16 to 17 and 64 to 512 numbers are the question's scenario, not book measurements. The book supplies the mechanism and the direction; the percentages here are arithmetic under stated assumptions (uniform hashing, balanced shares, unchanged layout).

A consistent-hashing ring maps keys and nodes into one circular space and gives each key to the first node clockwise, so a membership change should move about the joining or departing node's share rather than the whole keyspace.
The ~1/N moved fraction is an expectation under balanced load, not a guarantee: random token placement, unequal vnode counts and hot keys can move more, so the actual moved fraction must be measured.

Each token adds failure combinations and raises outage probability, while uneven token ranges produce uneven request load, so raising the vnode count is not a monotonic improvement in ownership safety.
A hot key remains a single hot key regardless of how many virtual nodes its owner holds, because tokens divide ring ranges and cannot split the authoritative workload of one key.

Node loss is absorbed by moving the lost node's ranges and load to survivors and repairing divergence later with anti-entropy, with hinted handoff only temporary protection, so higher token counts increase the repair and outage cost that must be bounded.
optional_claims: A membership change must record an ownership epoch and fence stale ownership, because a ring without epoch fencing can route one key to two owners during the change.

The choice rule favors consistent hashing only when membership churns and per-key movement must be bounded; a fixed node count favors modulo, range locality favors explicit ranges, and an unacceptable shared ring favors rendezvous hashing.
Ring operations and virtual-node tuning are themselves a cost that can exceed the movement they save, so the ring decision should be revisited when that cost dominates.

tasks.question: A dashboard computes each instance's p99 for a day and then averages those daily p99 values into a monthly figure. Why can the result understate the latency most requests experience, and what must be kept so the latency distributions can be merged correctly?
tasks.answer:
## 1. Direct answer

The monthly number is **not a p99**. It is the unweighted mean of per-instance, per-day p99 scalars. A percentile is a property of a distribution, not a linear statistic: the p99 of the pooled request population is not the average of the per-instance or per-day p99s. The average also gives each instance-day equal weight, while the pooled distribution weights each request; when the busiest instances or days have the worse tails, equal weighting dilutes them and the reported figure can sit below the latency threshold that the request population actually experiences. The error is not a guaranteed one-way bias: the same average can overstate the pooled p99 when slow instances or days carry little traffic, or when tail events are spread across different parts of the distribution.

To merge correctly, keep the **distributions, not the scalars**: per-bucket counts with known and compatible bucket boundaries (or the raw observations), together with observation counts/weights, the population definition, the observation window, metric identity and delta/cumulative temporality. Merge by summing counts into a common histogram (or pooling raw samples) and compute p99 **once** on the pooled distribution. Never average the p99 values, and never treat the average as a p99.

## 2. Facet matrix

Layer: **book** only. The question is about metric semantics and percentile aggregation; atlas cards and modeling-and-simulation artifacts are not evidence for it.

**Section-key abbreviations used below:** LEG1 = tycho.page.1c7350e3bc17483ba18f201d02727aea#1-specify-service-level-meaning-before-signal-collection; LEG5 = tycho.page.1c7350e3bc17483ba18f201d02727aea#5-downsampling-recording-rules-and-semantic-loss; RET5 = tycho.page.03bdffc1632345f390c2e845b52a3eb0#5-aggregation-loses-information-by-design; RET6 = tycho.page.03bdffc1632345f390c2e845b52a3eb0#6-failure-modes-and-operational-economics; MS2 = tycho.page.ecb28b2c14af4100b2d31e8f2aafcf56#2-measurement-types-and-aggregation-limitations; MS3 = tycho.page.ecb28b2c14af4100b2d31e8f2aafcf56#3-temporality-restarts-and-data-correctness; SLI3 = tycho.page.447ffb82d30f4a6999855c0a261e9a2a#3-measure-the-right-signals-at-the-right-level; TAIL1 = tycho.page.45935212b3b7476d8a163520f065b825#1-one-percentile-cannot-describe-a-distributed-request; ARR3 = tycho.page.bfa3a283746b42998825234aca63b101#3-define-denominators-and-avoid-coordinated-omission; LL = tycho.page.335682a8957c46d294535b5912762e91#architecture-little-s-law-is-an-average-identity; BC6 = tycho.page.180a25e8e7504ef4aa52257f76dbd1a8#6-decide-from-distributions-invariants-and-cost-together.

| # | Facet | Query formulations used | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|

| F2 | Request weighting: equal weight per instance/day versus request-weighted population | "request-weighted latency distribution across instances"; "observation counts"; "request volume weighting fleet latency" | LEG5, LEG1 |
| F3 | Observation boundary and fan-out: per-instance p99 is not end-to-end user latency | "p99 tail latency percentile distribution"; "one percentile distributed request" | TAIL1, SLI3 |
| F4 | Temporal rollup and peak loss: daily p99 plus monthly averaging smooths bursts and can make p99 look better | "downsampling"; "buckets"; "average latency hides tail percentile rollup" | LEG5, RET5, RET6 |
| F5 | Mergeable state: bucket boundaries plus counts, common schema, precision | "merge latency histograms percentiles across instances"; "histogram bucket boundaries merge"; "quantile estimation known bucket boundaries" | MS2, RET5, LEG5, SLI3 |
| F6 | Population, temporality and validity boundaries: windows, timeouts, retries, delta/cumulative, direction of error | "temporality"; "boundaries"; "denominators coordinated omission" | MS3, ARR3, MS2, LEG1 |

## 3. Mechanism and justification

### 3.1 The mathematical reason: a quantile is not a linear functional

Let each cell c = (instance i, day d) have n_c observations and CDF F_c. The pooled monthly CDF is

F(t) = sum over c of n_c * F_c(t) / sum over c of n_c.

The monthly p99 is the smallest t with F(t) at least 0.99. The dashboard computes

A = (1 / number of cells) * sum over c of Q_0.99(F_c).

There is no general identity A = Q_0.99(F). Equality is not general; it can hold in special cases, for example when all F_c are identical and all cells have equal n_c. The book states the same conclusion in several forms: "averaging percentiles across groups is generally invalid" (RET5); "the p99 of a globally pooled histogram is not an average of per-instance p99 values" (LEG1); and "a p99 computed from 5-minute buckets cannot be averaged to obtain the day's p99" (LEG5). A mean is a linear functional, so a sum and count can reconstruct it under compatible populations; a high-percentile distribution cannot be reconstructed that way (RET5). This is why the dashboard's monthly figure is not merely a slightly noisy p99: it is a different statistic.

### 3.2 The weighting reason: "most requests" are not "most instances"

Even if quantiles were linear, A weights every instance-day 1/(I*D), while the pooled distribution weights each observation equally through n_c. The book makes the analogous point for means: "An hourly mean of per-host means is not generally the fleet-wide mean unless correctly weighted by observation counts" (LEG5). A p99 average has the same defect, and the histogram counts are what carry the weights.

An invented arithmetic example makes the direction concrete. Suppose 99 low-traffic instances each receive 1 request and have p99 = 50 ms, while one busy instance receives 10,000 requests and has p99 = 500 ms. The equal-instance average is (99*50 + 500) / 100 = 54.5 ms. The pooled request distribution is almost entirely the busy instance, and its p99 is approximately 500 ms. The dashboard reports about 54.5 ms; the request population's tail threshold is about 500 ms. This is exactly the "understate the latency most requests experience" case: the one instance serving most requests is outvoted by many quiet instances. The numbers are illustrative arithmetic, not a measurement.

The reverse is equally possible: if the 500 ms instance is idle and the 50 ms instances serve the traffic, the equal-instance average can be far above the pooled p99. Thus the average is not guaranteed to understate; the direction depends on the correlation between traffic volume and tail latency, and on where the tail mass sits.

### 3.3 The observation-boundary reason: per-instance p99 is not user end-to-end latency

Each instance's p99 is a distribution at one observation point. A user request can touch several instances or dependencies, and the user experiences a maximum, sum or critical path, not one instance's marginal distribution. The book states that a percentile is a value of a distribution, not a single request's maximum, and that "p99 of the parent is not the sum of p99 of each child; nor is the p99 of a parallel fan-out equal to the p99 of one child" (TAIL1). Percentiles do not generally add. Therefore even a flawless merge of per-instance p99s would not reconstruct end-to-end latency under fan-out; the observation boundary has to be defined first (client-observed request, ingress-to-egress, queue wait, dependency call, or full job). A latency objective needs endpoint, time budget, observation point and outcome population (LEG1), and one recorded p99 without rejected or timed-out populations cannot prove user experience (SLI3).

### 3.4 The temporal-rollup reason: two layers of equal weighting

The dashboard applies a second equal-weight layer: first each instance's day becomes one p99, then each day becomes one thirtieth of the monthly figure. Pooling requests would weight each day by its request count. A short incident is diluted by the normal days in the average, and the book warns that "a daily series average can hide a 10-minute queue crisis" (RET5) and that rolling raw 10-second latency buckets into hourly averages "may erase evidence of short-lived user-visible incidents" (LEG5). Misconfigured downsampling can even make "p99 appear improved"; the required check is to "verify histogram/quantile mathematics and preserved boundary" (RET6). The point is not that every short event necessarily changes a monthly p99; it is that the averaged daily p99 is not the p99 of the month, and the double rollup can hide the tail mass that a pooled calculation would retain.

### 3.5 What must be kept so the distributions can be merged

The book's answer is a **histogram**, not a scalar percentile. A histogram is a bucket distribution of durations or sizes and supports estimable quantiles "under known boundaries" (MS2). To merge correctly, keep:

1. **Per-bucket counts and bucket boundaries.** These are the sufficient state for a pooled empirical CDF: sum counts bucket by bucket, then compute p99 once. Deleting buckets removes resolution for later quantile estimation (RET5). Raw observations are even better; if raw data is retained, pool the raw values and compute the quantile directly.
2. **A common bucket schema.** A histogram "aggregated without compatible bucket boundaries can misrepresent the merged distribution" (RET5). If schemas differ, re-bucket to a common (usually coarser) schema first; boundaries cannot be invented after the fact. Coarse buckets constrain the precision of the reconstituted percentiles (LEG5), so the merged figure must carry that precision limit.
3. **Counts/weights, not just percentages.** The merged CDF needs n_c per bucket or per cell; that is what makes the result request-weighted rather than instance-weighted. Sums and counts can reconstruct a mean under compatible populations, but they cannot reconstruct an arbitrary high-percentile distribution (RET5), so for quantiles the counts must be kept per bucket, not collapsed to a mean.
4. **Population and window semantics.** Keep the endpoint/operation class, observation point, start and end clock, observation window, and which events populate the histogram, including timeouts and never-started operations (ARR3, SLI3). Keep whether rejected, failed, retried or duplicate attempts are included; a success-only denominator can hide rejected operations. Keep whether values are raw, modeled, corrected, sampled or censored (ARR3).
5. **Metric identity and temporality.** A series name, value and timestamp are not enough: keep unit, resource scope, metric kind, attribute identity, aggregation temporality, and proper start/end semantics (MS3). Delta and cumulative points cover different intervals; merging overlapping ranges, missing intervals or multiple writers without handling that can double-count or create gaps (MS3).
6. **Raw data and correction assumptions.** If any coordinated-omission or missing-interval correction was applied, preserve both the raw data and the correction assumptions (ARR3). Corrected samples are modeled, not direct observations.
7. **Retention tiers and their limits.** Record what each tier cannot answer after downsampling. If coarse histograms are retained, the chosen schema bounds the precision; the retention design should preserve the resolution needed for the p99 question (LEG5, RET5).

A safe merge procedure is: define the population and window; normalize each source to a common bucket schema; sum counts per bucket and retain the total count; compute the p99 from the merged cumulative counts with a documented interpolation rule; if raw samples exist, pool them and compute the empirical quantile; validate a sample of merged results against raw data; and record the bucket resolution and sample size with the figure. If only p99 scalars remain, the distributions cannot be merged correctly; the honest output is "not mergeable from this state", not an average of the scalars.

## 4. Boundaries and trade-offs

- **The average can overstate as well as understate.** Equal weights over instances or days are not a one-way bias. If the slow cells are low-traffic, the simple average can exceed the pooled p99. A dashboard that always describes the average as conservative is wrong.
- **Equality is a degenerate case.** If every instance and day has the identical distribution and equal counts, the average of p99s equals the pooled p99. Real fleets rarely satisfy that, and the equality is fragile under any change in traffic mix or bucket boundaries.
- **An SLO stated as a proportion is different from a p99.** If the objective is "99% of eligible requests under X ms", the correct aggregate is a count of good and bad requests (sum numerators and denominators), not an average of p99s. The book's SLO material emphasizes eligible events, denominators and outcome populations. A percentile target is not interchangeable with a proportion target merely because both mention 99%.
- **Histograms are approximate.** Bucket boundaries and interpolation determine the estimate; a p99 from coarse buckets is not exact. Re-bucketing to coarser common boundaries loses resolution, and deleted buckets cannot be recovered. A mergeable sketch could be an alternative only if its merge semantics and error bounds are documented; the inspected sections establish the histogram/counts requirement, not a particular sketch.
- **Correct per-instance merging is still not end-to-end.** If requests fan out, a pooled per-instance histogram answers a per-instance question. User latency needs an end-to-end observation point, or a composition model with joint-distribution assumptions; percentiles do not generally add (TAIL1).
- **Population choices change the answer.** Timeouts, rejected requests, retries, duplicate attempts, unknown outcomes and success-only denominators all change what the "p99" means. The same numeric value can describe different populations and is not evidence of user experience by itself (SLI3, ARR3).
- **Window alignment and temporality matter.** Daily boundaries, rolling versus calendar months, time zones, delta versus cumulative points, overlapping ranges and missing intervals can all change the merge. A monthly figure assembled from misaligned windows is not the p99 of a defined month (MS3).
- **Sample size and tail stability.** A p99 needs enough tail observations to be stable; the book warns there is no universally magic p99 sample count and that temporal correlation affects interpretation (ARR3). A merged histogram with very few observations in the tail can produce a precise-looking but unstable figure.
- **A note on "most requests experience".** p99 is the slow-tail threshold, not typical latency; most requests are below it. The defensible claim is about the p99 of the request-weighted pooled distribution, not about the average request's latency. If the dashboard presents the averaged figure as "typical" latency, that is a second category error.

- The traffic distribution and the latency-volume correlation are unknown. They determine whether the equal-weight average understates or overstates the pooled p99. The "understate" outcome is most likely when the busiest instances or days have the worst tails, or when the same slow events affect many instances.
- The bucket schema is unknown. Without compatible boundaries and per-bucket counts, a correct merge is impossible; with only scalar p99s, the distributions cannot be recovered. The book does not prescribe a specific sketch or storage format.
- Fan-out is unknown. If requests touch multiple instances or dependencies, even a correct per-instance merge answers the wrong observation boundary; an end-to-end histogram or a composition model is required.
- No production dashboard, metric store or incident was inspected here. The book's examples are explicitly synthetic or conditional, and the legacy page's own evidence ledger disclaims executed measurements. Confidence is high in the conceptual conclusion (percentiles are not averageable; keep histogram counts/boundaries), high that equal weighting can understate a request-weighted tail, and only conditional on traffic and tail correlation for the direction and magnitude of the error.

core_claims: A percentile is not an additive statistic, so averaging per-day or per-instance p99 values does not yield the p99 of the combined population; the monthly figure is an average of group statistics, not a quantile of the month's requests.

Because each daily p99 is computed over that day's own population and the days are then averaged, short crises that a daily p99 already dilutes are diluted again, so the rollup can hide a 10-minute queue crisis and understate the tail the retained data actually supports.
Deleting or coarsening histogram buckets removes resolution needed to estimate quantiles later, and aggregating histograms without compatible bucket boundaries misrepresents the merged distribution.

Sum and count can reconstruct the mean under compatible populations but cannot reconstruct an arbitrary high-percentile distribution, so what must be kept is the bucket boundaries together with their counts, not a single plotted percentile value.

The pipeline must record where transform loss occurs and verify the histogram and quantile mathematics rather than trust the plotted p99; misconfigured downsampling appears in the failure table as an apparently improved p99.

One recorded p99 without the rejected and timed-out populations cannot prove user experience, so instrumentation must carry a logical operation ID spanning retries, attempt/admission/final outcome including explicit unknown and timeout, elapsed time, route and operation classification, and reconciliation outcomes after lost acknowledgments.
optional_claims: Retention and resolution should follow the question the telemetry must answer - real-time alert, incident diagnosis, historical capacity trend or audit need - and an audit obligation cannot be satisfied simply by retaining sampled telemetry.

Cardinality is multiplicative across labels, so an unbounded label such as raw URL or arbitrary client ID can saturate ingestion and storage; the synthetic catalogue therefore starts from bounded route/status histograms and a small gauge set rather than per-entity labels.
The synthetic catalogue comparison and its falsifiable test are proposed, not run, and the chapter reports no test data or result.

tasks.question: A scheduled availability probe passes for a checkout journey while customers receive rejects, and when the probe does fail the alert fires only after three successive failures. Why can a green probe coexist with a broken user journey, why does the retry rule suppress a real signal, and what must the probe declare before its result is used as evidence?
tasks.answer:
# Direct answer

A scheduled probe can stay green while checkout rejects because the probe measures a declared
contract, not the customer journey. Several gaps make the two observations compatible. The success
predicate can be weaker than the business outcome: an HTTP 2xx or a queue acknowledgement is not
a durable order, and the book treats the good event as a "durable domain result, not merely 2xx".
The probe's path can be narrower or privileged: a test identity, an allowlisted network origin, a
cached or stubbed dependency, or a route that skips the step which rejects customers. The probe
samples a population: one location, one payment method, one tenant, one moment, so a green
aggregate can hide a failing region or subpopulation. And attempts are not intents: a probe that
retries records eventual success, while a customer experiences the first attempt. The book states
the gap directly: "a probe is a measurement contract over a named journey, not a liveness
shortcut, and a shallow endpoint ping is not evidence for a complete journey", and "a green probe
does not prove a correct user journey".

The three-successive-failure retry does not measure failure; it filters runs. It exists because
most isolated probe failures are transient (the bound Azure availability-test note says "about 80%
of failures disappear on retry"), so a confirmation rule reduces false pages. But a
consecutive-failure counter resets on every success and fires only after a run of three. A real
partial or intermittent failure (one bad instance, one payment provider, one region, a dependency
failing a fraction of calls) produces exactly the non-consecutive pattern the counter discards.
The alert fires late (at least two probe intervals after onset), never fires for outages shorter
than the confirmation window, and never fires for a service failing a large fraction of attempts
without three back-to-back failures. The rule buys precision against probe noise by surrendering
recall against the dominant real failure mode, and it prices the trade as though a false page cost
more than a missed checkout outage.

Before its result is used as evidence, the probe must declare its measurement contract: who probes
and with which identity and credentials; what named journey and which steps and failure classes it
covers; from where and how often; what counts as success at the business level and within what
deadline; which population, numerator, denominator, window, aggregation, exclusions and data-source
revision the result belongs to; that the evidence is synthetic rather than production; and how
probe or credential failure is separated from product failure, including the false-positive and
false-negative boundary. The book's rule is to "bind who probes what, from where, how often, with
which identity, and what counts as success before the check is trusted". Without that binding a
green result is ambiguous between four states: the journey works, the probe bypassed the failing
step, the probe sampled a healthy subpopulation, or the probe measured no eligible operations.

## Facet matrix

| Facet | Decision it resolves | Strongest evidence |
|---|---|---|
| F1. Probe semantics: contract versus journey | What does a pass actually assert? | Synthetic Monitoring card; SLI walkthrough |
| F2. Coverage and population gap | How can green coexist with rejects? | Synthetic Monitoring owner notes; SLI population page; revision section |
| F3. Why the retry rule exists | What problem was it built for? | Synthetic Monitoring card and owner; health-check cards |
| F4. Why the rule suppresses signal | What does a run-length counter miss? | Synthetic owner; SLI alerting rules; incident evidence |
| F5. Alert-design boundary | Where is confirmation legitimate? | Health-readiness card; circuit breaker; degradation; SLI/SLO card |
| F6. Evidence declaration | What must be declared before use? | Synthetic owner; SLI owner; incident practice and evidence; tracing |

## F1. A probe measures a contract, not the journey

The atlas defines the mechanism as exercising "a representative user journey from outside the
service", cites Google SRE's black-box definition ("Testing externally visible behavior as a user
would see it"), and concludes that a probe is "a measurement contract over a named journey, not a
liveness shortcut". The condition list makes the contract explicit: the "probe identity, target,
locations, frequency and success criteria should be explicit", and a representative journey must be
probeable with known coverage and triaged false positives.

The contract's weakest link is usually the success predicate. The SLI chapter's table separates
"Correct within deadline" from "Durable domain result, not merely 2xx", and lists "Queue
acknowledgment called final reservation" as an unacceptable substitution. It also shows the inverse
failure: counting only 2xx responses among requests "admitted into the service", excluding
pre-handler overload rejections, "can report misleading health". A checkout probe that asserts HTTP
200 at the edge has measured admission, not the order. If payment authorization, inventory
reservation or confirmation is the step that rejects customers, a probe that stops at 200 measures a
prefix of the journey while customers experience the suffix. (Mapping the book's booking and
reservation examples onto checkout is my inference; the book's worked examples are explicitly
fictional.)

The honest statement is therefore not "the probe says checkout is fine" but "the probe says its
declared path returned its declared success at its declared time". The chapter purpose makes the
same point at dashboard level: "a green CPU dashboard cannot show that an authorized user completed
the intended operation or that a booking was not duplicated".

## F2. Why green can coexist with rejected customers

Green plus rejects is not a contradiction; it is two measurements of different populations. The
synthetic card's good-fit conditions require that "coverage/locations are known", which is another
way of saying that unknown coverage makes green uninterpretable. Five concrete mechanisms explain
the divergence.

1. Identity and origin. A probe identity that is allowlisted, privileged or synthetic tests a path
   customers do not have. The owner note records that Azure applies its retry rule "independently at
   each test location" and warns that availability tests use "shared IP addresses", so a firewall
   "must not rely on IP filtering alone". That same allowlisting is one way a green probe and
   blocked customers coexist: the probe is exempt from the control that rejects the customer.
2. Dependency path. An external journey check must be "independent of the dependency it observes",
   and the contraindication is an external check that "shares the dependency under test". A probe
   served by a cache, a healthy replica or a stubbed payment provider never touches the failing
   dependency; cached or missing health can also keep routing to a draining instance.
3. Aggregation. The revision section warns that "An unrelated region may hide under aggregate
   metrics" and asks for disaggregation by meaningful route or workload. A probe green in three
   locations and red in one, averaged, is green.
4. Denominator. The population page requires "Intent identity rather than HTTP attempt count across
   retries" and says a counter of attempted requests "is not the same denominator as successful
   unique booking decisions if clients retry". A probe's internal retry converts attempts into a
   success; the customer's intent has one attempt in their own experience. If the service also
   retries internally, the probe observes the post-retry outcome while the customer absorbs the
   pre-retry error and the retry budget (inference from the same denominator rule).
5. Empty or stale population. The burn-rate table lists "Zero observed errors at idle time" with the
   trap "Reporting '100% available' with no eligible operations". A scheduled probe at 03:00 with no
   demand is not evidence of availability under load, and a dashboard can show a stale green.

Some rejects are also the promised experience: a declined payment or a sold-out item can be a
correct business outcome, while a timeout or a 5xx is not. The population page insists that the
treatment of rejection classes be documented before measurement; a probe that classifies every
reject as success, or every reject as failure, cannot answer the question.

The resolution is comparative, not rhetorical: reconcile the two observations by comparing their
contracts (predicate, path, identity, population, window, version), not by deciding which observer
to believe. "A success-only denominator can hide rejected user operations, so a green dashboard may
not describe the promised experience."

## F3. Why the three-successive-failure rule exists

The rule is a debounce, not a detector. The bound Azure availability-test documentation retries a
failed test and reports "only if three successive attempts fail", while noting that "about 80% of
failures disappear on retry"; alerts are enabled by default. The design assumption is explicit:
single probe failures are usually noise, so confirmation reduces false pages at the cost of a
bounded delay. The card states the same trade as a contraindication: reject probes when "alert noise
exceeds signal".

The same run-length confirmation is standard where a false positive triggers a costly action and
another actor absorbs the failure. Health checks: "bound probe timeouts, require consecutive
failures and keep shared-dependency checks out of liveness." Load balancing: "AWS removes a target
after bounded consecutive failures and may fail open when all targets in all enabled Availability
Zones fail." Degradation: "Recovery needs hysteresis; Kubernetes compares flapping to hysteresis
and uses a stabilization window." Circuit breakers: the design requires "the rolling window,
minimum request volume and threshold comparison", and "open is a hypothesis, not recovery".

So the rule is not irrational; it is the right shape for a decision where waiting is cheap because a
replica, a pool or a traffic shift covers the gap. It is the wrong shape for product availability,
where nothing absorbs the failure: customers do.

## F4. Why the retry rule suppresses a real signal

The counter's statistic is run length, not failure rate, and that is why it discards real evidence.

- It resets on success. A service that fails two of every three probes has a permanently green
  board. Under an independence assumption, a service failing 40% of probe attempts has a 0.4 cubed
  (6.4%) chance of a three-run in any three-probe window; at 10% the chance is 0.1%. This is
  illustrative arithmetic, my inference, not a measurement; correlation changes the numbers but not
  the direction.
- It removes the transient class the vendor says is 80% of failures. "Disappear on retry" means the
  retry succeeded, not that the failed attempt did not happen. A customer who does not retry, or
  whose retry is not idempotent, experiences the discarded attempt.
- It changes what is measured. The probe now measures eventual success under the probe's retry
  policy, while the declared SLI is correct within deadline for an intent. Those are different
  quantities; the probe cannot replace the SLO without redefining the SLI.
- It adds detection latency and a blind window. With a probe every T and three successes required,
  no alert can occur before roughly 2T after onset, plus evaluation time and any alert-level "for"
  clause. An outage shorter than that window never alerts at all; the first evidence is a customer
  complaint, a support queue or lost orders. The incident log calls this detection uncertainty and
  separates occurrence from discovery.
- Per-location independence compounds it. Requiring three consecutive failures "independently at
  each test location" means a global fault that manifests intermittently at every location still
  fails to produce a run at any one of them; if the alert requires several locations to agree, the
  delay and the miss probability multiply.
- Two hysteresis layers can stack. Probe-level confirmation plus an alert-level for or
  keep_firing_for clause compounds the delay. The SLO card lists "window mismatch, flapping alerts
  and missing evaluations" as common failures, and a missed rule evaluation is a real blind spot,
  not a success.
- The error asymmetry is mispriced. The rule is tuned against false pages from probe noise. In
  checkout the false negative is lost orders. Nothing in the probe's contract says a missed outage
  is cheaper than a spurious page, so the tuning is a choice, not a derived result.

The rule can be kept as a page filter; it must not be the only product signal. The SLO guidance is
to "alert on user-visible burn, not raw 2xx counts; use multiwindow burn-rate rules with bounded for
and keep_firing_for; treat missed rule evaluations as a monitoring gap". A rate over a window
accumulates intermittent failures; a run-length counter hides them.

## F5. Where the counter is legitimate, and what replaces it

- Liveness, readiness and traffic removal: a false restart or ejection is harmful, and other
  capacity covers the gap; require consecutive failures and keep shared dependencies out.
- Circuit breakers: use a rolling window, minimum request volume and threshold; open is a
  hypothesis, not recovery.
- Degradation: use a stabilization window so a mode does not flap.
- Product availability: the SLI is a ratio of good events to total events over a window, the SLO is
  a target, and alerts should follow burn. "multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerting" is the
  Workbook's recommended technique, and the Prometheus for clause waits for persistence of a rate
  condition, not of a run of probe failures.

There is a sample-size trap on the replacement too: the fast-burn row warns against an "alert
threshold selected without enough valid event samples". A one-per-minute probe yields a tiny
denominator; a probe-only burn-rate alert can be as misleading as the consecutive counter, for the
opposite reason. That is an argument for real-user or internal signals where they exist: the
atlas's choice rule is to "prefer a synthetic probe only when no real traffic exercises the
journey".

The alert also needs an action contract. The SLO card says "a target without an owner, window or
action is a dashboard number, not an SLO"; the synthetic-budget section says to "record the signal,
source/alert version, decision and follow-up owner".

## F6. What the probe must declare before its result is evidence

Before the check is trusted, and before its output is used as evidence, the probe must declare:

1. Identity and origin: who probes, with which credentials and safe identity, and with an origin
   header; credential expiry is a configuration event, kept distinct from product alerts.
2. Journey and scope: the named journey and the steps it covers, and which failure classes it does
   and does not exercise. A shallow endpoint cannot stand for a complete journey. The SRE Book's SLI
   template asks "Which requests are included", citing black-box monitoring jobs as an example.
3. Location and path: from where, and whether the check is independent of the dependency under
   test. Shared IPs and firewall allowlists must be declared, because they can exempt the probe from
   the control that rejects customers.
4. Frequency, sampling and window: how often, how many samples, over which window; missed
   evaluations are monitoring gaps.
5. Success predicate: the business-level good outcome, the deadline, and how retries and attempts
   relate to intents. Pending or unknown is not success; a queue acknowledgement is not the final
   reservation.
6. Population and version: numerator, denominator, aggregation and exclusions fixed before
   measurement and published with the data source. A later change is a new SLO version, not a
   rewrite of the score; the data-source revision and effective date travel with the number.
7. Evidence class and limits: synthetic, not a production observation; coverage and sampling
   declared; a gap is unknown, not success; what the probe cannot see, including probe blindness and
   any dependency it shares.
8. Failure semantics: separation of probe failure from product failure, detection uncertainty, and
   the false-positive and false-negative boundary. A rehearsal must state "which user
   journey/failure classes were exercised and which were not" and "what signal triggered response,
   including false-positive/false-negative boundaries".
9. Action: which decision the signal triggers and who owns it.

The single sentence that compresses the requirement is the atlas rule: "bind who probes what, from
where, how often, with which identity, and what counts as success before the check is trusted".
Evidence discipline makes the same demand of any observation: the incident log needs "timestamp,
source, scope, first symptom and detection uncertainty" for detection, and "trace/sample/record
revision, window, metric definition, access limitations" for observation, because "a graph or quote
must be re-verifiable". A probe result without those fields is an anecdote; with them it is evidence
whose scope can be checked against the claim.

## Boundaries and trade-offs

- Genuine contradiction. If the probe truly asserts a durable, business-level outcome over the same
  population, path, identity classes and window, then green plus rejects is a contradiction to
  investigate: look for sampling, aggregation, clock or version mismatch, and reclassify the rejects.
  The design-gap explanation is not available when the declarations exclude it.
- Legitimate rejects. A declined payment, an out-of-stock item or a fraud block can be the promised
  experience. A probe that treats them as failures over-alerts; one that treats them as successes
  under-alerts. The classification must be declared before measurement, not chosen after the score.
- Synthetic is still right when no real traffic exercises the journey (pre-launch, a rare path).
  Then green is evidence about the path, not about demand or the population.
- Run-length confirmation is still right where an action is debounced and another actor absorbs the
  failure. The objection here is to using it as the only product detection statistic, not to
  hysteresis itself: keep_firing_for and a bounded "for" are legitimate anti-flap and
  false-resolution controls when the underlying signal is a rate.
- Statistical caveat. Independence is unrealistic; a hard dependency outage produces correlated
  failures and does reach three in a row. That is precisely the limitation: the rule catches total,
  sustained outages and misses partial, intermittent ones. The claim concerns the shape of the
  missed class, not every failure.
- Low sample. A probe-only burn rate on few events per window is weak evidence; the fast-burn trap
  applies. Fewer, rarer probes are not automatically safer evidence.
- Security. The black-box exporter "makes requests to any target it is given"; probe identity and
  credentials are themselves an attack surface and must be scoped. This is secondary here but part
  of the probe's declaration.
- What the sources do not establish. The atlas sources are public documentation, not benchmarks or
  production observations; the book's worked examples are fictional; and "no probe, canary or
  availability test was created or run". The 80% figure is a vendor statement about that vendor's
  availability tests, not a measured property of any reader's probe. No alert latency, burn rate or

tasks.question: An operator flips a feature-flag kill switch during an incident, but some replicas keep serving the feature, one replica falls back to an enabled default, and a permission check elsewhere was implemented as a flag. Why does the switch apply unevenly, why must a permission decision not inherit the flag's cache policy, and what must the snapshot, evaluation and lifecycle guarantee?
tasks.answer:
# Q235 — Kill-switch skew, fail-open defaults, and permission caching

## Direct answer

A kill switch is a new configuration revision, not an atomic command delivered to every
replica at once. Each process evaluates against the snapshot it has installed; replicas
install revisions at different times, disconnected workers keep old snapshots, and
in-flight requests pin the snapshot they started with. The fleet converges; it does not
switch at one instant. A replica that cannot evaluate must return its default, so an
enabled default turns a failure into a silent enable — the opposite of a kill switch. A
permission check is an authorization decision, not a feature toggle: it must be
authoritative or an explicit short-lived capability, must fail closed, and must not reuse
the flag's eventual-refresh/last-known-good cache policy, because a stale allow is an
authorization failure, not a cache miss. The configuration snapshot must be immutable,
whole, versioned, compatible and age-bounded; evaluation must be pinned, fail-safe,
observable and audited; and the lifecycle must have an owner, defined scope and expiry, an
owned kill switch, evidence-gated promotion, audited changes, compatible recovery and
removal.
