## 1. Why the kill switch applies unevenly

A flag selects behavior; it does not make the change simultaneous. The owner page states
the premise directly: 'A feature flag selects behavior; a dynamic parameter changes an
operating limit. Neither becomes simultaneous merely because its value sits outside a
binary.' [S2] The unit of change is a versioned snapshot, not a command. Processes fetch at
different times, disconnected workers retain old snapshots, and a reader installs a
complete snapshot atomically; it never assembles a request's limits from several revisions.
[S2] A replica that has not installed the kill-switch revision is not disobeying the
switch; it is still on its previous snapshot.

Even a converged fleet can still serve the feature to in-flight work. A request pins its
snapshot until completion; a long workflow explicitly chooses whether each step pins the
original behavior or re-evaluates current policy, and that choice must survive retries.
[S3] A kill switch changes the snapshot for new evaluations; it does not retroactively
rewrite work already pinned to the old snapshot.

The operator therefore needs convergence telemetry, not a belief. Record the revision
actually used in metrics, logs and asynchronous work [S3]; report the observed revision and
snapshot age when a process cannot refresh [S4]; and gate operations on the share of
processes actually on the intended revision [S4]. Serving an old value is a deliberate
policy for that decision class, not evidence of convergence. [S4] Without revision and age
data, 'some replicas keep serving' is indistinguishable from a failed publish.

This is why a kill switch is a bounded-staleness control, not a global transaction. The
owner page's three decision classes make the bound explicit: optional behavior may use
eventual refresh with last-known-good; a resource limit may use bounded staleness with a
conservative ceiling; a permission or irreversible action needs an authoritative decision
or an explicit short-lived capability. [S2] A flag control plane cannot promise atomicity it
does not have.

## 2. Why one replica fell back to an enabled default

The fallback itself is required: on abnormal execution, evaluation returns the caller's
default and must not throw. [S7] The defect is the value of the default. The owner page's
rule is explicit: 'on evaluation failure the default must be the safe branch, not a silent
enable.' [S7] The atlas good-fit condition says 'the default fails safe' [S1], and the
runbook says 'make the safe branch the default (disabled, deny or no exposure).' [S7]

An enabled default turns every failure into an enable: no provider, a missing flag, a type
mismatch, no matching filter, or an incompatible snapshot. [S7] The public behavior quoted
in the owner section treats absence as disabled in one SDK and returns a fallback with an
ERROR reason in another; the shared rule is that the fallback must be the safe branch. [S7]
If the replica's local default is enabled, it is fail-open, and the kill switch cannot be
relied on.

The reason must be visible. The provider state STALE means 'the provider's cached state is
no longer valid and may not be up-to-date with the source of truth', and the reason means
'the resolved value is non-authoritative or possibly out of date.' [S7] Tycho's rule is to
record key, version, scope, default, reason and snapshot age with each evaluation. [S7] A
fallback 'on' must never be reported as a normal 'on'; otherwise the operator cannot tell a
deliberate enable from an evaluation failure.

A silent enable is a silent correctness change. Graceful degradation says silent loss of
correctness is worse than an explicit failure; each mode needs an entry condition, a
visible status, an owner and an audited override. [S18] On that evidence, the enabled
default fails the tests for a kill-switch fallback: it is not visible, not owned, and not
audited as a failure mode.

The diagnosis is therefore: the replica's default is part of the flag definition or its
local binary configuration, and it is set to the unsafe branch. The fix is not to suppress
the fallback; it is to make the default disabled, deny or no exposure, make it consistent
across replicas, and surface the reason and age. [S7]

## 3. Why a permission decision is not a flag

A flag gates feature exposure. It does not evaluate principal, resource, action and
context; it does not establish authority; it does not grant a permission. The atlas card
makes this a hard contraindication: reject when a toggle 'is asked to grant a permission or
approve an irreversible action.' [S1] The owner page states the invariant: 'A flag may gate
a feature, but it never grants a permission, approves an irreversible action or substitutes
for an authorization decision; when authority cannot be established, the protected action
fails closed.' [S7]

Authorization belongs at the resource boundary: every request is authenticated and
authorized using principal identity, workload/device posture, policy and least privilege;
deny by default; fail closed when authority cannot be established. [S9] The decision
components are separate: a policy decision point evaluates policy and attributes, a policy
enforcement point applies the decision, a policy information point supplies attributes, and
a policy administration point manages policy. [S8] A flag collapses those into a
configuration value and a flag-write permission; that is a design inference from the
separation, not a source claim.

If the permission check is behind a flag, the flag can skip the check; that is a bypass.
The check must run unconditionally on the protected path, and the flag may only control
whether the feature is exposed after authorization. This follows from 'never replace an
authorization check' [S7] and 'every request is authenticated and authorized at the resource
boundary' [S9]; the 'unconditionally' phrasing is my design inference.

Least privilege requires a bounded scope, an owner, a revocation path and audit. [S10] A
flag has an owner and a change log, but not an entitlement model: it does not revoke a
principal's access, and its change log is not a decision log. [S19, S17] An unexplainable
allow or deny is a production incident, not a policy detail. [S8] A flag value cannot
explain why this principal may perform this action on this resource now.

## 4. Why a permission decision must not inherit the flag's cache policy

The owner page separates three decision classes and gives each its own propagation and
failure contract. [S2]

| Decision class | Suitable propagation contract | Failure policy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Optional interface behavior | Eventual refresh with a last-known-good snapshot | Use a documented local default |
| Concurrency or resource limit | Bounded staleness with a conservative ceiling | Stop expansion when the snapshot expires |
| Permission or irreversible action | Authoritative decision or explicit short-lived capability | Reject when authority cannot be established |

The page then states the consequence: 'The last row cannot safely inherit the first row's
convenient cache policy. A flag is also not a substitute for an authorization check.' [S2]
That is the direct answer to the cache question.

The flag cache is a freshness claim, not a consistency theorem. A cache-aside read is
bounded by the fill revision, the invalidation path and the TTL; a reader can briefly see
stale data after a write; a lost invalidation is unbounded without a TTL; a TTL bounds but
does not eliminate staleness. [S11] The cache guidance is consistent: a cache is fit only
when consumers can tolerate a bounded stale window, and it is rejected when stale reads
violate a hard contract. [S12] Stale-while-revalidate is rejected when stale data would
mislead a decision, and TTL is rejected when data must be current. [S13, S14]

For a permission, the stale window is a security window. A stale allow survives revocation
until refresh; a stale deny blocks a legitimate action; an enabled default grants on
failure. The RBAC owner page states the consequence directly: 'a stale attribute is an
authorization failure, not a cache miss,' and attribute sources need freshness SLAs. [S8]
The cache page is equally direct: even a TTL cache may expose stale authorization;
sensitive or security-related data should be retrieved from the primary source; bypass
caching or require strict verification for revocation-sensitive operations; 'a copied
permission bit is not its own authority.' [S11]

The permission path therefore needs its own contract: an authoritative decision at the
enforcement boundary, or an explicit short-lived capability that is scoped, time-bound,
revocable and auditable, and that fails closed. [S2, S9] A capability is not a flag
snapshot: its TTL is part of the authorization semantics, its revocation is enforced, and
its issuance is a decision, not a background refresh. [S2] It may cache, but not with the
flag's policy: not last-known-good, not eventual refresh, not an enabled default, and not a
per-replica value that can diverge into an allow.

Three inherited policies are wrong: the failure policy (default versus deny), the freshness
policy (bounded staleness versus authority), and the audit policy (change history versus
decision logging). [S2, S8, S17] That is why the permission decision must not inherit the
flag's cache policy.

## 5. What the snapshot must guarantee

- Immutable and identified. Every snapshot has a monotonically increasing revision, a
  payload digest, an activation policy and a minimum compatible binary version. [S2, S3]
- Whole and atomic. A reader installs a complete snapshot atomically; it never assembles a
  request's limits from several revisions. The acceptance checks require whole-snapshot
  reads, nondecreasing accepted revisions and no unsupported record format. [S2, S6]
- Age-bounded and observable. Bound snapshot age separately for each decision class; report
  the observed revision and snapshot age when a process cannot refresh; alert on stale data.
  [S4, S6, S7]
- Pinned. A request pins its snapshot until completion; a long workflow explicitly chooses
  whether each step pins the original behavior or re-evaluates current policy, and that
  choice must survive retries. [S3]
- Integrity and idempotency. If publication succeeds but the publisher loses the response,
  retry using the publication identifier and compare the digest. [S4]
- Compatible and recoverable. The minimum compatible binary version and activation policy
  are the compatibility gate; an old binary must not apply a snapshot it cannot interpret; a recovery revision
  has a higher revision than the one it replaces, even when its behavior resembles an older
  one. [S2, S3]
- The kill switch is a value in a new revision, not an out-of-band mutation. That is a
  design inference: the snapshot is the unit of change [S2], and the request pins that
  snapshot [S3].

## 6. What evaluation must guarantee

- Stable inputs. The evaluation path needs a stable flag key, an evaluation context, a
  version, a default and an observable reason. [S7]
- Pinned and deterministic. Evaluation is against the pinned snapshot; the same snapshot
  and the same context produce the same decision, and a request does not mix revisions.
  Determinism is a design inference from atomic installation and request pinning. [S2, S3]
- Non-throwing and fail-safe. Evaluation must not throw; it returns the default on abnormal
  execution, and that default must be the safe branch. [S7]
- Non-authoritative on staleness. A stale or error result is not current authority; the
  reason must say so, and the failure contract handles it. [S7]
- Observable and audited. Record the key, version, scope, default, reason and snapshot age
  with each evaluation; make every override attributable to a member and a diff; the atlas
  card requires evaluation to be observable. [S1, S7]
- Distinguishable states. A provider error, a deliberate off state, a cohort exclusion and a
  stale snapshot must not collapse into the same value; the reason is part of the result.
  [S7, S4]
- A kill switch with a safe branch. The runbook uses an owned kill switch for emergency
  shutoff and makes the safe branch the default (disabled, deny or no exposure). [S7] That
  the kill switch must win over ordinary exposure rules is a design inference; the evidence
  requires the switch to be owned and the safe branch to be the default. [S1, S7]
- A separate permission path. Permission evaluation is not a flag evaluation; it must be an
  authoritative decision or a short-lived capability and must fail closed. [S2, S9]

## 7. What the lifecycle must guarantee

- Ownership, scope, expiry and a kill switch. The atlas good-fit condition requires toggle
  ownership, expiry, scope and kill switch to be defined, and the default to fail safe. [S1]
- Evidence-gated promotion and a freeze path. The lifecycle model is validated -> canary -> broad, with an alarm able to freeze either stage ->
  frozen -> recovery -> canary; promotion requires evidence; an alarm freezes
  expansion; a compatible recovery revision must itself be observed. These are proposed
  lifecycle states, not a particular product API. [S3]
- Audited changes. Record revisions in metrics, logs and asynchronous work; make overrides
  attributable to a member and a diff; keep an append-only, attributable audit log and
  reject logs that the actor can mutate or delete. [S3, S7, S17]
- Temporary versus permanent. Temporary flags expire and are removed after their purpose; a
  permanent toggle becomes configuration with an owner, review cadence, audit trail and
  removal date; remove the toggle after the rollout. [S5, S7]
- Recovery that respects durable effects. Recover by publishing a higher, compatible
  revision and re-observing it; a binary rollback does not undo durable effects already
  produced while the flag was on; recovery may need draining jobs, dual-format readers or
  data repair. [S4, S7, S15]
- No promotion without telemetry. If telemetry is absent, pause promotion rather than
  interpreting no samples as success. [S4]
- For a permission decision, the flag lifecycle is the wrong lifecycle. It belongs to the
  policy lifecycle: policy administration, revocation, attribute freshness and decision
  audit. That is a design consequence of the separation, not a source claim. [S8, S9]

## 8. Boundaries and trade-offs

- A kill switch is not instantaneous, and a snapshot flag cannot make it so. If the
  requirement is 'no request after time T uses the feature', the flag snapshot is the wrong
  mechanism; use a synchronous authoritative check, drain traffic, or revoke a capability.
  This is a design inference from the bounded-staleness contract. [S2, S5]
- Last-known-good is a feature, not a bug, for optional behavior. It is a bug for a
  permission: the evidence explicitly says the permission row cannot inherit the optional
  row's cache policy. [S2]
- A short-lived capability is a legitimate compromise. It bounds revocation delay at the
  cost of issuance, expiry and clock handling; it is acceptable only when it is scoped,
  revocable, auditable and fail-closed. [S2, S9]
- A flag may gate exposure of a feature that is separately authorized, and it may select
  which policy engine evaluates (a dark launch). It may not be the permission decision or
  the condition that skips the check. This is a design inference from 'never replace an
  authorization check' and the resource-boundary rule. [S7, S9]
- If the flag system actually provides deny-by-default, revocation, decision audit and
  freshness SLAs, then it is a policy decision point and the objection is about the
  contract, not the word 'flag'. That is a design inference. [S8]
- The sources are public documentation and Tycho synthesis; no flag was evaluated, no
  canary, kill switch or rollback was executed, and no production incident was observed.
  The atlas card is source-linked but partial-bounded and self-checked, not independent
  review or promotion. [S1, S7]
- The scenario is underdetermined. The enabled fallback could be a missing flag, a provider
  error, a type mismatch, an incompatible binary, or a local default. The fix is the same,
  but the diagnosis needs the evaluation reason and snapshot age. [S7, S2, S6]

## 10. Unknowns and confidence

Unknowns:

- The flag system's propagation mechanism, polling/streaming interval and snapshot-age bound
  are not given; the answer states the contract, not a product setting.
- The exact trigger of the enabled default is not given. It could be a missing flag, a
  provider error, a type mismatch, an incompatible binary or a local default; the evaluation
  reason and age are needed to distinguish them.
- Whether the permission flag is the decision itself or a gate in front of a separate check
  is not given. The answer rules out both as an authorization decision, but the remediation
  differs.
- No numeric freshness SLA for permissions follows from the sources. The evidence says stale
  attributes are authorization failures and requires freshness SLAs; it does not set a value.
- The sources do not benchmark products or establish production behavior; the atlas card is
  partial-bounded and self-checked.

Confidence:

- High that an enabled default is fail-open and violates the kill-switch contract: the atlas
  and owner page say the default must fail safe and must not silently enable. [S1, S7]
- High that a permission decision must not be a flag or inherit the flag's cache policy: the
  owner page states the separation and the cache table explicitly, and the RBAC and cache
  pages state the stale-authorization consequence. [S2, S8, S11]
- High that the snapshot, evaluation and lifecycle contract is the right shape: multiple
  sections agree on revisions, atomic installs, pinning, age bounds, audit and removal.
  [S2, S3, S4, S7]
- Medium on the exact operational mechanism for a hard cutoff; the sources describe the
  trade-off but do not prescribe a product pattern. [S2, S5]

What would change the answer:

- A separate authorization check behind the flag, with the flag only gating exposure, would
  make the flag acceptable as an exposure control but not as the decision.
- A flag system that is actually an authoritative policy decision point, with
  deny-by-default, revocation, decision audit and a freshness SLA, would satisfy the contract
  under a different name.
- A requirement that tolerates a bounded stale authorization window would permit a
  short-lived capability, but not the flag's indefinite last-known-good cache.
core_claims: A kill switch is an asynchronous distributed transition: processes fetch at different times and disconnected workers retain old snapshots, so some replicas can keep serving the old value, and staying there is a deliberate policy rather than evidence of convergence.

Each reader must install a complete versioned snapshot atomically, with a monotonically increasing revision, payload digest, activation policy and minimum compatible binary version, instead of assembling a request's limits from several revisions, and it must report its observed revision and snapshot age.

Evaluation failure must return a documented default that fails safe; a fallback to an enabled default defeats the kill switch, and a process that cannot refresh must report its revision and snapshot age rather than have its old value read as convergence.

A permission or irreversible action is a separate decision class that needs an authoritative decision or an explicit short-lived capability and must reject when authority cannot be established; it cannot inherit the optional-behavior cache policy, because a flag is not a substitute for an authorization check.

The flag lifecycle must guarantee an owner, expiry, defined scope and kill switch, observable evaluation with an audit trail for overrides, bounded snapshot age, and removal after rollout, because permanent flags become configuration debt and a flag that hides a broken deployment should be rejected in favor of a canary or branch by abstraction.

Publication must validate schema and cross-field constraints, record an immutable revision and select a stable exposure cohort, and promotion must require evidence: absent telemetry pauses promotion rather than counting as success, and a request pins its snapshot until completion while a long workflow states whether each step pins the original behavior or re-evaluates, surviving retries.
optional_claims: Operational gates should include error rate, latency, resource use, data correctness signals, cohort sample size and the share of processes actually on the intended revision, and recovery may require draining jobs, dual-format readers or data repair in addition to a flag change.
A lost publication response is retried using the publication identifier and a digest comparison, and a failed publisher must not sit on the critical request path for ordinary cached behavior.
Exposure percentage measures eligibility rather than traffic or risk, and a small cohort can contain the most expensive tenant.

judge_0.notes: Covers the distributed transition, fail-safe default, permission-decision separation, and snapshot/evaluation/lifecycle guarantees, with only publication schema and cohort detail thin.

judge_1.notes: Covers skew, fail-open defaults, permission separation and lifecycle controls, but omits stable exposure-cohort selection, schema/cross-field publication validation and the canary/branch-by-abstraction rejection, leaving two core claims partial.

tasks.question: A scenario contract omits constraints entirely and still validates. Why can it be a valid scenario while being unable to support a decision record that claims to respect hard constraints?
tasks.answer:
# Q247 - A scenario contract that declares no constraints, and a decision record that claims hard-constraint respect

## 1. Direct answer

A scenario contract is a reproducibility contract for an experiment, not a certificate of decision fitness. In the V12 contract the constraints property is mandatory, but its array has no minimum length, so a scenario that declares no constraints still passes schema validation and the structural gate. Validation therefore answers "is this a well-formed, referenced, hash-consistent scenario?" and not "does this scenario establish anything about a decision?".

A decision record's claim to respect hard constraints is a different kind of statement: a relation between a declared constraint set, a set of candidates and per-constraint evidence. Hard constraints do work only by eliminating candidates. With no constraint set behind the claim, the relation has no left-hand side: every candidate satisfies every constraint vacuously, the claim is true but empty, and it cannot separate a candidate that meets a cost ceiling from one that exceeds it. That is why the scenario can be valid and still unable to support the record: validity is about reproducible inputs, support is about a declared constraint set plus per-constraint evaluation. When the scenario declares nothing, it supplies the former and none of the latter.

One precision on the premise, because it changes what is being asserted. I checked the shipped contract: constraints is in the schema's required list, and a scenario document with the property deleted fails validation with "'constraints' is a required property"; the same document with constraints: [] validates with zero errors. So the exact true formulation is: a scenario can declare no constraints at all in content (an empty list) and still validate. Literal property omission is not valid in v1; if a later contract version drops the key, the same conclusion follows a fortiori.

## 2. Facet matrix

| # | Decision-relevant facet | Query formulations used | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | What a scenario contract certifies (reproducible experiment, comparability) | "scenario contract constraints"; "scenario with no constraints"; "scenario still a scenario decision support" | tycho.page.dedc5f2d31912a9ba5f562a86009fda0#overview; #required-structure; #the-identical-workload-rule |
| 2 | What validation actually checks, and why an empty list passes | "scenario validation schema"; "structural validity is not evidence"; "constraints empty declared none" | tycho.page.6fd0d561e3e2900dc8b59a3011071cd2#v12-a-structural; tycho.page.dedc5f2d31912a9ba5f562a86009fda0#required-structure |
| 3 | Experiment validity versus decision fitness (gate separation) | "validation what the schema proves"; "decision-supported status evidence insufficient" | tycho.page.6fd0d561e3e2900dc8b59a3011071cd2#the-gate-matrix; #v12-e-decision-validity; #what-the-gates-do-not-establish; #a-gate-flow |
| 4 | What the decision record owes when it makes the claim | "decision record hard constraints"; "constraint evaluation pass fail not-tested"; "hard constraints declared candidate eliminated" | tycho.page.c7a43944f1d41e810eec0d17ec33b85a#required-structure; #hard-constraints-versus-preferences; tycho.page.6fd0d561e3e2900dc8b59a3011071cd2#v12-e-decision-validity |
| 5 | Why the claim collapses without a declared set (vacuity, scope, laundering) | "constraint laundering decision record"; "vacuous satisfaction empty constraint set decision"; "scenario constraints versus decision constraints scope" | tycho.page.dedc5f2d31912a9ba5f562a86009fda0#failure-modes; #business-comparable-metrics; tycho.page.c7a43944f1d41e810eec0d17ec33b85a#failure-modes; #why-a-decision-record-is-not-a-score |
| 6 | The honest outcomes and the legitimate use of a constraint-free scenario | "exploratory scenario without decision claim"; "validation what the schema proves" | tycho.page.ea9adae8cf8a3196a3515d383b075f53#a-checklist-for-insufficient-evidence; #insufficient-evidence-is-not-a-model-failure; tycho.page.c7a43944f1d41e810eec0d17ec33b85a#insufficient-evidence-is-a-result; tycho.page.b0c704c825b2faf15a1d118dc9a6b1cc#validity-limits |

## 3. Mechanism and justification

### 3.1 What a valid scenario certifies (facet 1)

The scenario page states its own purpose: it fixes the model identifier, workload, candidate configuration, uncertainty inputs, replication count, seed scheme, metrics and constraints, and for a candidate comparison the workload, duration, warmup, metric definitions and seed scheme are identical while only the configuration changes (#overview). Its required structure lists every field, including constraints as hard, soft and non-quantitative (#required-structure). The identical-workload rule treats the shared hard constraints as one of the dimensions that make A/B/C comparable, next to the horizon, arrival process, metric units and seed scheme (#the-identical-workload-rule).

So a scenario certifies: the same experiment was run, the inputs are fixed, and the comparison is reproducible. The constraint entry is a dimension of that comparability record, not a proof about any candidate. When the list is empty, the identical-workload rule is satisfied trivially (all candidates share the empty set), the run and result contracts still apply, and nothing in the scenario contract becomes false. The scenario remains a valid scenario - the book says exactly that: "A scenario with no constraints is still a scenario" - but the same sentence ends with the consequence, "but it cannot support a decision record that claims to respect hard constraints" (#required-structure).

### 3.2 What "validates" actually checks (facet 2)

The structural gate is explicit about its scope. V12-A checks frontmatter, unique volume/chapter/page and model/scenario/run/decision identifiers, that every scenario model_id resolves, that runs resolve to models and scenarios, that decision candidates resolve to runs, that pattern identifiers and owner pages resolve, that stored hashes match, that the reverse index is derived rather than hand-edited, and the iron rule about no V12 references outside the V12 directory (#v12-a-structural). Nothing in that list asks whether a constraint list is non-empty or whether its statements are decision-relevant. The validator's scenario branch applies exactly the schema, the hash and the model reference (scripts/validate_v12.py), so no constraint check exists at either level.

The schema matches that scope. Its required array includes constraints, so the key must exist; the constraints value is an array whose item schema requires id, kind and statement, with no minItems. By contrast, metrics and validity_limits carry minItems 1 (schema artifact schemas/v12/scenario-specification.v1.schema.json). I verified the consequence directly against the shipped schema with a JSON Schema validator: the original order-intake scenario produced zero errors, the same document with constraints: [] produced zero errors, and the same document with the key deleted produced the required-property error. An empty constraint list is therefore a documented shape rather than a loophole: the contract admits it while still demanding that the scenario say something about metrics and validity limits.

That asymmetry is what "still validates" means: validation is conformance plus reference integrity plus hash consistency. It is not a judgment that the scenario contains the inputs a decision needs.

### 3.3 Experiment validity is not decision fitness (facet 3)

The gates are deliberately separate: V12-A structure, V12-B model correctness, V12-C statistical validity, V12-D calibration, V12-E decision validity, V12-F independent review (#the-gate-matrix). The gate flow says a later gate cannot substitute for an earlier one (#a-gate-flow); the converse - that passing V12-A does not confer V12-E - follows from the same separation, though I did not find a sentence that states it in those words. The page lists what the gates do not establish: that source claims are true, that models match a real system, that decisions are accepted by the owner, that CI or production behavior is proven, and that any pattern is promoted (#what-the-gates-do-not-establish). The contract family is described as making gaps visible rather than replacing source evidence, calibration, security review or owner acceptance (tycho.chapter.3a47e8385cccb8a2ce764bfa765cc740#boundaries-and-evidence).

V12-E is where the constraint obligation lives, and it is a property of the decision record: candidates and their runs, hard/soft/non-quantitative constraints, business-comparable metrics with units, evidence statuses, an explicit recommendation or a no-recommendation outcome, non-quantitative constraints kept separate, reversal triggers and limitations (#v12-e-decision-validity). A scenario is never asked to be decision-sufficient; a decision is asked to declare and evaluate its constraints.

### 3.4 What the record owes when it claims constraint respect (facet 4)

The decision-record contract requires constraints (hard, soft and non-quantitative), candidates with scenario and run references, metrics, evidence, an outcome with a rationale and non-quantitative constraints, reversal triggers, limitations and pattern links (#required-structure). The example excerpt shows the operative form: a constraint has an id, a kind and a statement such as cost <= 3.0, and the outcome names a recommendation; the record is decision-supported under those declared constraints (#example-excerpt). The shipped decision schema makes the obligation hard: constraints has minItems 1, and constraint_evaluation has minItems 1 with a constraint_id, a status of pass, fail or not-tested, and an evidence string. A record cannot validate with no constraints at all.

The semantics explain why. A hard constraint is a condition a candidate must satisfy: candidate C is eliminated by a cost ceiling even if it has the best success rate; a soft constraint is tradeable; a non-quantitative constraint is one the model cannot measure (#hard-constraints-versus-preferences). In the worked checkout record, C is eliminated by cost and p95 latency, B and A pass the declared constraints, B wins on success rate and cost per success, A wins on latency as a tradeoff rather than a failed constraint, no undeclared success threshold is applied, and because the operability constraint remains unverified the recommendation is conditional. The claim is always scoped: decision-supported under its declared constraints.

### 3.5 Why the claim collapses when the scenario declares no constraints (facet 5)

Three mechanisms, all visible in the sources.

Vacuity. "Respects hard constraints" is a universal statement over the declared set. Over an empty set it is true for every candidate, including one that would blow a cost ceiling if a ceiling existed. A statement that cannot fail carries no discriminating information, and the purpose of a hard constraint is exactly to discriminate - to eliminate C despite its best success rate (#hard-constraints-versus-preferences). The record would look supported while doing none of the work that a decision record exists to do: the record's own rationale is that a weighted score can hide weights and trade a hard constraint away, and that constraints, evidence statuses and unknowns are kept in separate fields precisely to prevent that (#why-a-decision-record-is-not-a-score).

Scope. The claim is relative to a declared set, so the set has to come from somewhere. The shipped decision schema requires at least one constraint and at least one evaluation entry (minItems 1), so the set cannot simply be absent. Either the record declares the constraints itself - and then the support is the record's constraint_evaluation evidence, not the scenario, which contributes runs and inputs but no constraint satisfaction - or it points at the scenario's constraint list as its source, and that pointer lands on an empty list. A scenario with no constraints can be cited as the experiment behind a recommendation; it cannot be cited as the thing the recommendation respects.

Laundering. When the set is absent or imported after the fact, the known failure modes appear by name. The scenario page lists constraint laundering: a hard cost ceiling becomes a soft preference after a candidate fails it, and the record must show the constraint and the failure (#failure-modes). The decision page lists recommendation without constraints, score laundering and evidence inflation (#failure-modes). The neighbouring rule makes the same point for a different declared quantity: a decision record that uses a metric not declared in the scenario is a validation failure (#business-comparable-metrics). The constraint case is the same principle, but the scenario contract cannot enforce it, because there is nothing in the scenario to compare against.

### 3.6 The honest outcomes (facet 6)

Insufficient evidence is a first-class result. The decision contract says a record with recommendation none can still be insufficient-evidence and is not invalid (#required-structure), and it devotes a section to the modernization record that returns insufficient evidence rather than forcing a recommendation (#insufficient-evidence-is-a-result). The checklist is concrete: return insufficient evidence when a hard input is assumed and its range spans the decision boundary, when a hard constraint cannot be evaluated by the model, when a confidence interval straddles pass and fail, when candidates are indistinguishable, when validity limits exclude the operating condition, when rollback is unrehearsed, or when the ranking is contested (#a-checklist-for-insufficient-evidence). A scenario that declares no constraints cannot evaluate any constraint, so under that checklist the honest status is insufficient-evidence or proposed, never decision-supported. A conditional decision is allowed only when the missing evidence is explicitly non-quantitative and the record can state the condition - the checkout record's unverified operability constraint is the model case (#a-checklist-for-insufficient-evidence; #hard-constraints-versus-preferences).

The validity-limits page gives the general form of the same rule: a validity limit is not a disclaimer appended to a result, it is a condition on the result's use, and if a decision needs the omitted mechanism the model is outside its domain (#validity-limits). A decision that needs constraints and reads a constraint-free scenario is in the same position. The calibration page adds the parallel for values: a parameter can change status only with new evidence, and repeating an assumed value in a decision record does not make it measured (#the-four-statuses). Repeating a constraint in a decision record does not make the scenario declare it.

## 4. Boundaries and trade-offs

- Literal versus content omission. Property omission fails the shipped schema; an empty list passes. The question's premise is true for content and false for the literal property, and the answer above keeps that distinction rather than smoothing it.
- A constraint-free scenario is not a defective artifact. It is a valid experiment record and is the right shape for exploration, stress and sensitivity work where no candidate is being selected. In the shipped artifact set, five of ten scenarios are referenced by no decision record at all (order-intake baseline and saturation, checkout sensitivity, overload and convergence stress), while the two decisions reference only the five candidate scenarios. The fault is not the empty list; it is using that scenario as the support for a constraint claim.
- A contract gap I could observe but not attribute. The checkout decision declares C1-C5, while every checkout and modernization scenario declares C1-C3, and the constraints that actually eliminate candidate C - the cost ceiling C4 and the p95 ceiling C5 - exist only in the decision record. The validator applies schema checks to scenarios and then checks only that the decision's constraint ids equal its own constraint_evaluation ids; it does not compare them with the referenced scenario's constraints. So the decision-to-scenario constraint chain is unenforced in the implementation. The book does not state a matching rule either, so I report this as a gap in the contract, not as a defect proven against a written requirement.
- What the evidence does not license. Sargent supports the verification/validation and data/conceptual/operational distinction, and the contracts page says the schemas are original V12 contracts with no conformance claim and no replacement for source evidence, calibration, review or owner acceptance. None of this certifies a real system, and a model-verified engine is not a validated system.
- Non-quantitative constraints are the legitimate hard case. They may be declared and remain not-tested (the operability constraint C3 in the checkout record), with the recommendation marked conditional. That is a declared-but-unverified constraint, which is different from an absent constraint: the record can name what is unverified and what would change the outcome.
- Reversal triggers cut both ways. A decision supported under declared constraints must name what would reopen it, and the constraint set supplies the thresholds to trigger on (arrival rate, cost ceiling, latency ceiling). A constraint-free scenario offers no threshold, so the record's trigger has to come from elsewhere - further evidence that the support is not in the scenario.
- A tentative decision is legitimate. A proposed record may precede constraint declaration; the status enum admits proposed. What is not legitimate is decision-supported on a constraint set that the scenario never declared.

## 6. Unknowns and confidence

- The unenforced link is the main unknown. No section I read requires a decision record's constraint identifiers to match the constraints of the scenario it references, and the shipped artifacts do not match (decision C1-C5 versus scenario C1-C3, with C4 and C5 existing only in the decision). I therefore treat "cannot support" as a semantic and evidentiary relation that the contract describes but does not mechanically enforce. A validator rule tying the two sets would make the unsupported case detectable; its absence means the case is invisible to V12-A.
- The retrieval layer returned a single section for most queries, so the absence of a dedicated section on empty-constraint scenarios is not proof that none exists (the book layer's own boundary: zero results do not prove absence). I did not search the full text for such a section; the cited sections are the ones that answered the facets.
- I did not inspect corpus, qrels, labels, answers or rankings, by instruction; no claim here depends on what the benchmark expects.
- Confidence is high on the two mechanical facts (the empty list validates; the key cannot be deleted) because I executed the schema check, and high on the book's explicit sentence about a constraint-free scenario. It is medium on how a reviewer should disposition the gap, because the sources supply statuses and checklists for decisions but no rule for scenario records used as decision support.
- What would change the answer: a contract version with a minimum constraint count on scenarios would make the premise false; a cross-record reference rule would make the unsupported claim a validation failure rather than a silent one; and a section stating that scenario constraints are advisory would weaken the support argument for scenarios that do declare them.
core_claims: The scenario schema requires every field - identity, workload, configuration, uncertainty, replications and seed, metrics, constraints, evidence status and validity limits - and a scenario with an empty constraints list is still a structurally valid scenario.
Structural validity is not decision sufficiency: the same contract states that a scenario with no constraints cannot support a decision record that claims to respect hard constraints.

A hard constraint is a condition a candidate must satisfy and it eliminates candidates that fail it, a soft constraint is a tradable preference, and a non-quantitative constraint is a condition the model cannot measure that is kept separate.

The decision-record contract requires declared hard, soft and non-quantitative constraints alongside candidates and runs, metrics with units and a business-comparable flag, evidence statuses, an explicit recommendation or none, reversal triggers and limitations.

V12-E decision validity checks exactly those declarations, so a record that claims to respect hard constraints while its scenario declares none has no declared basis, cannot show which candidates were eliminated, and fails the gate even though both artifacts validate structurally.

Constraint laundering - turning a hard cost ceiling into a soft preference after a candidate fails it - is a named failure mode that the record must expose, and a decision record using a metric not declared in the scenario is a validation failure.
optional_claims: The identical-workload rule requires the same horizon, warmup, arrival process, metric definitions and seed scheme across candidates, with only the candidate configuration varying; a comparison that changes the workload is invalid.
A record with recommendation none can still be an insufficient-evidence outcome and is not an invalid record.
A metric mismatch such as using p99 latency while the scenario declares p95 causes the validator to reject the decision record.
